newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine sugar mills welcome import restriction.
newsitem.headline: Philippine sugar mills welcome import restriction.

text.p: Philippine sugar millers welcomed on Friday the government's order to stop imports of the commodity to shore up domestic sugar prices.
"We welcome this move. This is necessary to stabilise local sugar prices," said Jose Maria Zabaleta, executive director of the Philippine Sugar Millers Association.
Philippine Sugar Regulatory Administration (SRA) chief Wilson Gamboa said on Friday he had ordered traders and millers not to import sugar for the next six months because of a glut.
"We will ask the Bureau of Customs not to release any imported sugar that comes in between now up to March 1997," Gamboa told Reuters in a phone interview.
Traders said the SRA has "the regulatory power" to restrict imports of the commodity.
"The United States is doing it, why can't we do it? Japan and Europe also do not allow agricultural imports without government permission," an executive in a local sugar mill told Reuters.
Gamboa said the Philippines imported 1.23 million tonnes of sugar from September 1995 to July 1996, resulting in an excess of 423,000 tonnes.
Local traders imported sugar in the last crop year ending August because of domestic production shortfall.
But Gamboa said a surplus 423,000 tonnes was imported.
"We (have) sugar up to our ears," Gamboa told reporters.
Local sugar prices dropped to a low of 525 pesos per 50 kgs two weeks ago from a high of 800 pesos last year because of the imported sugar, Gamboa said.
"The over-importation of sugar in the country was an abuse of trade liberalisation," one trader told Reuters.
Traders said refined sugar swamped the market after the Philippines offered a 35 discount on tariffs to exporters from neighbouring countries.
The tariff discount on imported refined sugar was part of the country's commitment under the ASEAN Free Trade Area (AFTA), said one trader.

"Indonesia made a similar offer but it withdrew the discount five or six months ago. The Philippines should also do the same to save its local sugar industry," said another executive Philippine sugar mill.
Traders said most of the imported refined sugar that swamped the local market came from Thailand.
"Imported raw sugar also came from Brazil and Australia," said one trader.
Gamboa said his agency had ordered the export to the United States of 78,000 tonnes of locally grown sugar from October to December this year to reduce the country's sugar stocks.
Sugar planters and traders were also asked to ship to the United States "at the earliest possible time" some 53,000 tonnes scheduled for delivery from January to March 1997.

The Philippines benefits from a programme under which developing nations export sugar to the U.S. at premium prices. The USDA announced last month it cut the Philippines' raw cane sugar allocation by 8.4 percent to 219,059 tonnes for the 1996/1997 crop year from the previous 237,422 tonnes.
